rows.subtopic: Electric Field and Field Lines
rows.stem: A thin plastic rod is bent into a circular ring of radius R. It is uniformly charged with charge density \(\lambda\). The magnitude of the electric field at its centre is :
rows.solution:
The ring is charged UNIFORMLY, and that symmetry settles the question before any integration.
Take any small element of the ring. It sets up a field at the centre directed along the line joining it to the centre. Now take the element diametrically OPPOSITE it: it carries exactly the same charge, sits at exactly the same distance R, and its field at the centre points in exactly the OPPOSITE direction.
The two cancel. Every element of the ring can be paired off this way, so the contributions cancel in pairs and
\(E_{centre} = 0\)
The magnitude of the electric field at the centre is ZERO.
Note that the POTENTIAL there is not zero: potential is a scalar and the contributions add rather than cancel, giving \(V = \dfrac{\lambda 2\pi R}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R}\). A vanishing field alongside a non-vanishing potential is exactly what symmetry produces here.

rows.subtopic: Energy Stored in a Capacitor
rows.stem: Ten capacitors, each of capacitance 1 \(\mu\mathrm{F}\), are connected in parallel to a source of 100 V. The total energy stored in the system is equal to :
rows.solution:
Capacitors in PARALLEL add directly, so ten capacitors of \(1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) give
\(C = 10 \times 1\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 10\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{F}\)
In parallel every capacitor carries the full source voltage, so the energy stored is
\(U = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10^{-5} \times (100)^{2}\)
\(U = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10^{-5} \times 10^{4} = 5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{J}\)
The total energy stored is \(5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-2}\) J.
The same ten capacitors in SERIES would give only \(0{\cdot}1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) and store a hundredth as much at the same voltage, which is the trade the parallel connection avoids.

rows.subtopic: Cells, EMF and Internal Resistance
rows.stem: Consider the circuit shown in the figure. The potential difference between points A and B is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — two parallel branches drawn between nodes A and B, each branch a cell in series with a resistor. EVERY numeric value (both emfs and both resistances) and the cells' relative polarity appear only in the drawing; the stem names none of them, so the question is unanswerable from text. Described: that there are two parallel branches between labelled nodes A and B, each carrying one cell and one resistor. Withheld: the four values and the polarity sense, which are exactly what the question tests. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The two cells are connected in PARALLEL between the same pair of points A and B, each with its own internal resistance. Nothing is drawn from the terminals, so the potential difference across them is simply the EQUIVALENT EMF of the combination:
\(\varepsilon_{eq} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\varepsilon_{1}}{r_{1}} + \dfrac{\varepsilon_{2}}{r_{2}}}{\dfrac{1}{r_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{r_{2}}}\)
Substituting \(\varepsilon_{1} = 12\) V with \(r_{1} = 1\ \Omega\), and \(\varepsilon_{2} = 6\) V with \(r_{2} = 0{\cdot}5\ \Omega\):
\(\varepsilon_{eq} = \dfrac{\dfrac{12}{1} + \dfrac{6}{0{\cdot}5}}{\dfrac{1}{1} + \dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}5}} = \dfrac{12 + 12}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{24}{3} = 8\ \mathrm{V}\)
The potential difference between A and B is 8 V.
It is NOT the average of 12 and 6, which would be 9, because the cells are weighted by their CONDUCTANCES: the 6 V cell has half the internal resistance and therefore twice the say. A circulating current of 4 A flows round the loop between the two cells, discharging the 12 V one and charging the 6 V one, and it is that current which drags the common terminal voltage down to 8 V.

rows.subtopic: Torque on a Current Loop and Magnetic Dipole
rows.stem: A loop carrying a current I clockwise is placed in \(x - y\) plane, in a uniform magnetic field directed along z-axis. The tendency of the loop will be to :
rows.solution:
The field is directed along the z-axis and the loop lies in the x-y plane, so the field is PERPENDICULAR to the plane of the loop, that is parallel to its axis. This is the one orientation in which no turning effect arises: the magnetic moment is already aligned with the field, so \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{m} \times \vec{B} = 0\).
What remains is the force on each element, \(d\vec{F} = I\,d\vec{l} \times \vec{B}\). Since \(d\vec{l}\) lies in the plane and \(\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to it, each force is perpendicular to both, and so lies IN the plane of the loop, directed along the radius.
Every element is pushed radially, and all in the SAME sense, because the current and field directions are the same all the way round. So the loop is squeezed uniformly inwards and its tendency is to SHRINK.
Nor can it translate: the radial forces are symmetric about the centre and sum to zero, so there is no net force and the options describing motion along an axis are ruled out. A loop in a UNIFORM field can be deformed or turned, never displaced.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: A 10 cm long wire lies along y-axis. It carries a current of \(1{\cdot}0\) A in positive y-direction. A magnetic field \(\vec{\mathrm{B}} = (5\ \mathrm{mT})\hat{j} - (8\ \mathrm{mT})\hat{k}\) exists in the region. The force on the wire is :
rows.solution:
Use \(\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})\), with the length vector along the current:
\(\vec{L} = (0{\cdot}10\ \mathrm{m})\hat{j}, \qquad \vec{B} = (5\ \mathrm{mT})\hat{j} - (8\ \mathrm{mT})\hat{k}\)
\(\vec{F} = 1{\cdot}0 \times \left[(0{\cdot}10\hat{j}) \times (5 \times 10^{-3}\hat{j} - 8 \times 10^{-3}\hat{k})\right]\)
Take the two terms separately. The first vanishes, since \(\hat{j} \times \hat{j} = 0\): the component of the field ALONG the wire exerts no force at all. The second uses \(\hat{j} \times \hat{k} = \hat{i}\):
\(\vec{F} = 1{\cdot}0 \times 0{\cdot}10 \times (-8 \times 10^{-3})\,\hat{i} = -8 \times 10^{-4}\,\hat{i}\ \mathrm{N}\)
\(\vec{F} = -(0{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{mN})\hat{i}\)
The force is \(0{\cdot}8\) mN directed along the negative x-axis. Forgetting to convert 10 cm into metres inflates this by ten and produces the 80 mN distractors.

rows.subtopic: The Moving Coil Galvanometer
rows.stem: A galvanometer of resistance G \(\Omega\) is converted into an ammeter of range 0 to I A. If the current through the galvanometer is \(0{\cdot}1\%\) of I A, the resistance of the ammeter is :
rows.solution:
A galvanometer becomes an ammeter when a small SHUNT S is placed in parallel, so that most of the current bypasses the coil. At full scale the two branches share the same potential difference:
\(I_{g}G = (I - I_{g})S\)
Here \(I_{g} = 0{\cdot}1\%\ \text{of}\ I = \dfrac{I}{1000}\), so \(I - I_{g} = \dfrac{999I}{1000}\):
\(\dfrac{I}{1000}G = \dfrac{999I}{1000}S \quad\Longrightarrow\quad S = \dfrac{G}{999}\)
The RESISTANCE OF THE AMMETER is that of the two in parallel, not the shunt alone, and that is the step the question is really testing:
\(R_{A} = \dfrac{GS}{G + S} = \dfrac{G \cdot \dfrac{G}{999}}{G + \dfrac{G}{999}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{G}{999}}{\dfrac{1000}{999}} = \dfrac{G}{1000}\)
The resistance of the ammetre is \(\dfrac{G}{1000}\ \Omega\). Stopping at the shunt gives \(\dfrac{G}{999}\), which is the distractor on offer; a good ammeter must have a very LOW resistance so that inserting it in series barely disturbs the circuit.

rows.subtopic: AC Voltage Applied to an Inductor and a Capacitor
rows.stem: The reactance of a capacitor of capacitance C connected to an ac source of frequency \(\omega\) is ‘X’. If the capacitance of the capacitor is doubled and the frequency of the source is tripled, the reactance will become :
rows.solution:
The reactance of a capacitor is
\(X_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}\)
so it is inversely proportional to BOTH the capacitance and the frequency. Doubling C and tripling \(\omega\) therefore divides the reactance by \(2 \times 3 = 6\):
\(X' = \dfrac{1}{(3\omega)(2C)} = \dfrac{1}{6}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{X}{6}\)
The new reactance is \(\dfrac{X}{6}\).
The physical content is that a capacitor opposes SLOW changes and passes rapid ones: at high frequency the plates never have time to charge up enough to push back, so the reactance falls, and a larger capacitance takes more charge for the same voltage, which lowers it further.

rows.subtopic: Displacement Current
rows.stem:
In the four regions, I, II, III and IV, the electric fields are described as :
Region I : \(\mathrm{E}_x = \mathrm{E}_0 \sin (kz - \omega t)\)
Region II : \(\mathrm{E}_x = \mathrm{E}_0\)
Region III : \(\mathrm{E}_x = \mathrm{E}_0 \sin kz\)
Region IV : \(\mathrm{E}_x = \mathrm{E}_0 \cos kz\)
The displacement current will exist in the region :
rows.solution:
Displacement current exists wherever the ELECTRIC FLUX is CHANGING WITH TIME:
\(i_{d} = \varepsilon_{0}\dfrac{d\phi_{E}}{dt}\)
so the test to apply to each region is simply whether its field expression contains t.
REGION I has \(E_{x} = E_{0}\sin(kz - \omega t)\), which depends on t. The flux through any area changes as the wave passes, so a displacement current exists here.
REGION II has a CONSTANT field, so \(\dfrac{dE}{dt} = 0\).
REGIONS III and IV have fields varying with position z but NOT with time; they are static patterns, frozen in place.
So the displacement current exists only in the region whose field is a travelling wave, region I. What matters is variation in TIME, not in space, and the three static options are there to catch a reader who sees a formula with a variable in it and stops looking.

rows.subtopic: Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: The transition of electron that gives rise to the formation of the second spectral line of the Balmer series in the spectrum of hydrogen atom corresponds to :
rows.solution:
The Balmer series consists of all transitions that END on \(n_{f} = 2\), which is what puts it in the visible region.
Its lines are counted outwards from the longest wavelength:
FIRST line (\(H_{\alpha}\)): \(n_{i} = 3 \to n_{f} = 2\)
SECOND line (\(H_{\beta}\)): \(n_{i} = 4 \to n_{f} = 2\)
THIRD line (\(H_{\gamma}\)): \(n_{i} = 5 \to n_{f} = 2\)
So the second spectral line of the Balmer series corresponds to \(n_{f} = 2\) and \(n_{i} = 4\).
The option with \(n_{f} = 3\) belongs to the Paschen series, and \(n_{i} = \infty \to n_{f} = 2\) is the SERIES LIMIT, the shortest wavelength of the Balmer series rather than its second line.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors
rows.stem: Ge is doped with As. Due to doping,

options.label: A
options.text: the structure of Ge lattice is distorted.

options.label: B
options.text: the number of conduction electrons increases.

options.label: D
options.text: the number of conduction electrons decreases.

rows.solution:
Arsenic is PENTAVALENT, carrying five valence electrons where germanium has four. Four of them form the covalent bonds with the neighbouring germanium atoms; the fifth is left over.
That fifth electron is bound only loosely, needing about \(0{\cdot}01\) eV to be freed, which thermal energy at room temperature supplies easily. It is therefore released into the crystal as a CONDUCTION ELECTRON, and the arsenic atom becomes a fixed positive donor ion.
So doping with arsenic INCREASES THE NUMBER OF CONDUCTION ELECTRONS, making the crystal n-type.
The number of holes does not increase; it FALLS, because the mass-action law \(n_{e}n_{h} = n_{i}^{2}\) holds at a given temperature, and the extra electrons raise the recombination rate. Nor is the lattice distorted: arsenic substitutes for germanium at a lattice site, which is why doping works at all.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: Two beams, A and B whose photon energies are \(3{\cdot}3\) eV and \(11{\cdot}3\) eV respectively, illuminate a metallic surface (work function \(2{\cdot}3\) eV) successively. The ratio of maximum speed of electrons emitted due to beam A to that due to beam B is :
rows.solution:
Einstein's equation gives the maximum kinetic energy in each case, and the speeds follow from it.
BEAM A: \(K_{A} = 3{\cdot}3 - 2{\cdot}3 = 1{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{eV}\)
BEAM B: \(K_{B} = 11{\cdot}3 - 2{\cdot}3 = 9{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Since \(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\) with the same electron mass in both cases, the speed goes as the SQUARE ROOT of the kinetic energy:
\(\dfrac{v_{A}}{v_{B}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_{A}}{K_{B}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1{\cdot}0}{9{\cdot}0}} = \dfrac{1}{3}\)
The ratio of the maximum speeds is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\).
The trap is to compare the kinetic energies directly and answer \(\dfrac{1}{9}\). Note too that the work function must be SUBTRACTED first: the ratio of the photon energies, \(\dfrac{3{\cdot}3}{11{\cdot}3}\), plays no part.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Wave Nature of Matter
rows.stem: The waves associated with a moving electron and a moving proton have the same wavelength \(\lambda\). It implies that they have the same :
rows.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength depends on one quantity only:
\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\)
so two particles sharing the same wavelength necessarily share the same MOMENTUM, whatever else differs between them.
Nothing else follows. Their SPEEDS cannot be equal, since \(p = mv\) and an electron is about 1836 times lighter than a proton, so at equal momentum the electron moves that many times faster. Their ENERGIES cannot be equal either, since \(K = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m}\) makes the lighter particle by far the more energetic. ANGULAR momentum does not enter at all: it depends on the path, and none is specified.
So equal wavelength implies equal momentum, and that is the whole of what it implies.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect and its Experimental Study
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : In photoelectric effect, the kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons increases with increase in the intensity of the incident light.
Reason (R) : Photoelectric current depends on the wavelength of the incident light.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are FALSE.
The ASSERTION is false because it attaches the kinetic energy to the wrong variable. Einstein's equation, \(K_{max} = h\nu - \phi_{0}\), contains the FREQUENCY and the work function, and no term for intensity. Raising the intensity sends MORE photons per second, so more electrons are emitted and the photocurrent rises, but each photon still delivers the same energy \(h\nu\), so the kinetic energy of the emitted electrons is unchanged. This independence of intensity was one of the classical wave theory's decisive failures.
The REASON is false as stated. The photoelectric CURRENT is proportional to the number of photons arriving per second, that is to the INTENSITY of the light, and for a given intensity above threshold it is essentially independent of wavelength. Wavelength governs the ENERGY of the electrons, not how many of them there are.
So the two statements between them swap the roles of intensity and frequency, which is exactly the confusion the photoelectric effect exists to clear up.

rows.subtopic: Inductance
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The mutual inductance between two coils is maximum when the coils are wound on each other.
Reason (R) : The flux linkage between two coils is maximum when they are wound on each other.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
The ASSERTION is TRUE. Mutual inductance measures how effectively a changing current in one coil induces an emf in the other, and it is greatest when the two are wound one on top of the other on a common core.
The REASON is also TRUE and is precisely why. Mutual inductance is defined through the flux linkage:
\(M = \dfrac{N_{2}\phi_{2}}{I_{1}}\)
so M is large exactly when a large fraction of the flux produced by the first coil threads the second. Winding the coils on each other leaves almost no path for flux to escape between them, so the linkage is as complete as it can be and M approaches its maximum value \(k\sqrt{L_{1}L_{2}}\) with the coupling coefficient k near 1.
Separate the coils, or turn one through a right angle, and much of the flux misses the second coil entirely; the linkage falls and M falls with it.
Both statements are true and the reason is the correct explanation. This is why a transformer's windings are placed on the same core rather than side by side.

rows.subtopic: Force Between Parallel Currents
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Two long parallel wires, freely suspended and connected in series to a battery, move apart.
Reason (R) : Two wires carrying current in opposite directions repel each other.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
The ASSERTION is TRUE. Two freely suspended parallel wires connected in SERIES to a battery do move apart.
The REASON is also TRUE: two wires carrying currents in OPPOSITE directions repel one another, the force per unit length being
\(\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I_{1}I_{2}}{2\pi d}\)
and it is the correct explanation, provided one sees why the currents ARE opposite. A series connection means the same current traverses both wires in turn: it goes out along one and returns along the other. So although a single current is flowing, its direction in the two wires is antiparallel, and antiparallel currents repel.
Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Had the wires been connected in PARALLEL instead, the current would run the same way in both, they would attract, and the wires would move together. The connection, not the battery, decides which way they swing.

rows.subtopic: Reflection by Spherical Mirrors
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Plane and convex mirrors cannot produce real images under any circumstance.
Reason (R) : A virtual image cannot serve as an object to produce a real image.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are FALSE, and the same oversight defeats them both: they forget that an object can be VIRTUAL.
The ASSERTION claims that plane and convex mirrors can never produce a real image. They can. If a CONVERGING beam falls on such a mirror, the incident rays are already headed towards a point behind it; that point is a virtual OBJECT, and the mirror reflects the beam to a real convergence point in front of itself. What is true is the weaker statement that for a REAL object these mirrors always give a virtual image, and the assertion has overstated it into a claim about all circumstances.
The REASON claims that a virtual image cannot serve as an object to produce a real image. It can, and routinely does in every multi-element instrument: the virtual image formed by one lens or mirror acts as the object for the next, and the final image may perfectly well be real.
Both the assertion and the reason are false.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of Resistivity
rows.stem: Find the temperature at which the resistance of a wire made of silver will be twice its resistance at 20°C. Take 20°C as the reference temperature and temperature coefficient of resistance of silver at 20°C = \(4{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\).
rows.solution:
The resistance of a metal varies with temperature as
\(R = R_{0}\left[1 + \alpha(T - T_{0})\right]\)
where \(R_{0}\) is the resistance at the reference temperature \(T_{0} = 20\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\).
The wire's resistance is to be DOUBLED, so \(R = 2R_{0}\):
\(2R_{0} = R_{0}\left[1 + \alpha(T - T_{0})\right]\)
Cancelling \(R_{0}\), which is why its value is never needed:
\(2 = 1 + \alpha(T - T_{0}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \alpha(T - T_{0}) = 1\)
\(T - T_{0} = \dfrac{1}{\alpha} = \dfrac{1}{4{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}} = 250\)
\(T = 20 + 250 = 270\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C} \qquad (543\ \mathrm{K})\)
The resistance of the silver wire doubles at \(270\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\).
Note that the temperature coefficient is quoted per KELVIN while the reference is in degrees Celsius, and that is harmless here: a RISE of 250 K is the same as a rise of \(250\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), since only the interval enters.

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem: Monochromatic light of frequency \(5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{14}\) Hz passes from air into a medium of refractive index \(1{\cdot}5\). Find the wavelength of the light (i) reflected, and (ii) refracted at the interface of the two media.
rows.solution:
(i) REFLECTED LIGHT. Reflection keeps the light in the SAME medium, so neither its speed nor its frequency changes, and therefore neither does its wavelength. The wavelength is simply that of the incident light in air:
\(c = \nu\lambda \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda = \dfrac{c}{\nu} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{14}}\)
\(\lambda = 6 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m} = 600\ \mathrm{nm}\)
(ii) REFRACTED LIGHT. On entering the medium the FREQUENCY is unchanged, because the boundary can neither create nor destroy wave cycles; what changes is the speed, \(v = \dfrac{c}{\mu}\). The wavelength shortens in the same proportion:
\(\lambda_{medium} = \dfrac{\lambda_{air}}{\mu} = \dfrac{600}{1{\cdot}5} = 400\ \mathrm{nm}\)
So the reflected light has a wavelength of 600 nm and the refracted light 400 nm.
The contrast is the point of the question: reflection changes nothing about the wave, while refraction changes the speed and the wavelength together but leaves the frequency, and hence the colour, alone.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A plano-convex lens of focal length 16 cm is made of a material of refractive index \(1{\cdot}4\). Calculate the radius of the curved surface of the lens.
rows.solution:
Apply the lens maker's formula to a PLANO-convex lens, remembering that the flat face has an infinite radius and therefore contributes nothing:
\(\dfrac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left[\dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}}\right]\)
With one curved surface of radius R and one flat surface:
\(\dfrac{1}{16} = (1{\cdot}4 - 1)\left[\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{\infty}\right] = \dfrac{0{\cdot}4}{R}\)
\(R = 16 \times 0{\cdot}4 = 6{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The radius of the curved surface is \(6{\cdot}4\) cm.
The radius comes out much SMALLER than the focal length here because the glass is of low refractive index: with \((\mu - 1) = 0{\cdot}4\) the surface has to be strongly curved to bend the light enough. The same lens made of \(\mu = 1{\cdot}5\) glass would need a radius of 8 cm for the same focal length.

rows.subtopic: Reflection by Spherical Mirrors
rows.stem: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature 40 cm. Find the (i) position of the image formed and (ii) magnification of the image.
rows.solution:
For a concave mirror the focal length is half the radius of curvature, and both are NEGATIVE under the Cartesian convention since they lie in front of the mirror:
\(f = \dfrac{R}{2} = \dfrac{-40}{2} = -20\ \mathrm{cm}, \qquad u = -30\ \mathrm{cm}\)
(i) POSITION. From the mirror equation:
\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)
\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{-30} = \dfrac{1}{-20} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{-3 + 2}{60} = -\dfrac{1}{60}\)
\(v = -60\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The image forms 60 cm in FRONT of the mirror, on the same side as the object, and since v is negative it is REAL.
(ii) MAGNIFICATION.
\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -\dfrac{-60}{-30} = -2\)
The magnification is \(-2\): the image is inverted, as the minus sign says, and twice the size of the object.
The result is the expected one for an object lying between the focus and the centre of curvature, 20 cm and 40 cm here: the image is real, inverted, magnified, and beyond the centre of curvature.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Wave Nature of Matter
rows.stem: Consider a neutron (mass m) of kinetic energy E and a photon of the same energy. Let \(\lambda_n\) and \(\lambda_p\) be the de Broglie wavelength of neutron and the wavelength of photon respectively. Obtain an expression for \(\dfrac{\lambda_n}{\lambda_p}\).
rows.solution:
Treat the two separately, because a photon and a neutron relate energy to momentum by different rules, and that difference IS the answer.
THE PHOTON has no rest mass, so its energy and momentum are related by \(E = pc\):
\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{p}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda_{p} = \dfrac{hc}{E}\)
THE NEUTRON is non-relativistic, so \(E = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m}\), giving \(p = \sqrt{2mE}\), and its de Broglie wavelength is
\(\lambda_{n} = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mE}}\)
Dividing one by the other, h cancels:
\(\dfrac{\lambda_{n}}{\lambda_{p}} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mE}} \times \dfrac{E}{hc} = \dfrac{E}{c\sqrt{2mE}} = \dfrac{1}{c}\sqrt{\dfrac{E}{2m}}\)
which is more neatly written as
\(\dfrac{\lambda_{n}}{\lambda_{p}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{E}{2mc^{2}}}\)
The ratio depends on the energy through a square root, so the two wavelengths are NOT simply proportional. Since \(mc^{2}\) for a neutron is about 940 MeV, the ratio is tiny for ordinary energies: a neutron of a few electronvolts has a wavelength far shorter than a photon of the same energy.

rows.subtopic: Electric Current and Ohm's Law
rows.stem:
Plot a graph showing the variation of current with voltage for the material GaAs. On the graph, mark the region where :
(a) resistance is negative, and
(b) Ohm's law is obeyed.
rows.solution:
GRAPH. Plot current I in milliamperes against voltage V. The curve for GaAs is not a straight line: it rises from the origin, at first in proportion to V, then bends over to a maximum, then FALLS as the voltage is increased further, passes through a minimum, and finally rises again.
(a) REGION WHERE RESISTANCE IS NEGATIVE. This is the stretch between the maximum and the minimum, where the curve slopes DOWNWARDS: the current DECREASES as the voltage increases. Since the dynamic resistance is \(\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}\), a negative slope means a NEGATIVE resistance. Mark this falling portion.
(b) REGION WHERE OHM'S LAW IS OBEYED. This is the initial stretch nearest the origin, where the graph is a STRAIGHT LINE through the origin, so that \(V \propto I\) and the resistance is constant. Mark this rising straight portion.
The material is worth the attention the question gives it: the negative-resistance region is what allows a GaAs device to sustain oscillations and generate microwave power, which no ohmic material can do.

rows.subtopic: Electric Flux and Gauss's Law
rows.stem:
A cube of side \(0{\cdot}1\) m is placed, as shown in the figure, in a region where electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}} = 500\,x\,\hat{i}\) exists. Here x is in meters and E in \(\mathrm{NC^{-1}}\). Calculate :
(a) the flux passing through the cube, and
(b) the charge within the cube.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — a cube drawn on x, y, z axes with origin O marked and a dimension arrow labelled 0·1 m. The cube's POSITION along the x-axis relative to the origin is shown only in the drawing, and since the field is x-dependent the flux cannot be found without it. Described: that there are labelled x, y, z axes, an origin O and a cube with one 0·1 m dimension marked. Withheld: where the cube's faces sit relative to the origin. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
The field \(\vec{E} = 500x\,\hat{i}\) points along x and grows with x, so flux crosses only the two faces PERPENDICULAR to the x-axis. The other four faces have their area vectors perpendicular to the field, so \(\vec{E} \cdot \vec{A} = 0\) for each of them and they contribute nothing.
From the figure the left face is at \(x = 0{\cdot}1\) m and the right face at \(x = 0{\cdot}2\) m, and each has area \((0{\cdot}1)^{2} = 0{\cdot}01\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\).
(a) FLUX. For a closed surface the area vector points OUTWARDS, so the left face's points along \(-\hat{i}\) and the right face's along \(+\hat{i}\):
\(\phi_{L} = -\left[500 \times 0{\cdot}1\right] \times 0{\cdot}01 = -0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\)
\(\phi_{R} = +\left[500 \times 0{\cdot}2\right] \times 0{\cdot}01 = +1{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\)
\(\phi = \phi_{L} + \phi_{R} = 0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\)
The net flux is positive because the field is STRONGER where it leaves than where it enters, and it is that imbalance, not the field itself, that signals enclosed charge.
(b) CHARGE. By Gauss's theorem:
\(q = \phi\,\varepsilon_{0} = 0{\cdot}5 \times 8{\cdot}85 \times 10^{-12}\)
\(q = 4{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C}\)
Had the field been uniform, the two fluxes would have cancelled exactly and the enclosed charge would have been zero.

rows.subtopic: Drift of Electrons and Resistivity
rows.stem: Define ‘current density’. Is it a scalar or a vector ? An electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}\) is maintained in a metallic conductor. If n be the number of electrons (mass m, charge \(- e\)) per unit volume in the conductor and \(\tau\) its relaxation time, show that the current density \(\vec{j} = \alpha \vec{\mathrm{E}}\), where \(\alpha = \left(\dfrac{ne^2}{m}\right)\tau\).
rows.solution:
DEFINITION. Current density is the current flowing per unit area of cross-section taken NORMAL to the direction of flow:
\(j = \dfrac{I}{A}\)
SCALAR OR VECTOR? It is a VECTOR, its direction being that in which the positive charge carriers drift. Current itself, by contrast, is a scalar despite having a sense along the wire, because it does not obey vector addition; current density does, which is what lets it describe flow at a POINT inside a conductor of any shape.
DERIVATION. Consider a conductor of cross-sectional area A carrying n free electrons per unit volume, each of charge \(-e\) and mass m, in a field \(\vec{E}\).
Each electron experiences a force \(-e\vec{E}\), hence an acceleration \(-\dfrac{e\vec{E}}{m}\). Collisions interrupt this repeatedly, and if \(\tau\) is the average time between collisions the electrons acquire a steady DRIFT velocity
\(\vec{v}_{d} = -\dfrac{e\vec{E}\tau}{m}\)
In a time \(\Delta t\) every electron moves a distance \(v_{d}\Delta t\), so all the electrons within a cylinder of that length and cross-section A cross the far face. The charge transported is
\(I\Delta t = ne\,A\,|\vec{v}_{d}|\,\Delta t = \dfrac{ne^{2}A\tau}{m}|\vec{E}|\,\Delta t\)
Dividing by \(\Delta t\) and by the area, and writing \(I = |j|A\):
\(|j| = \dfrac{ne^{2}\tau}{m}|\vec{E}|\)
Since the drift velocity of the negative electrons is opposite to \(\vec{E}\) while the conventional current is along it, the two vectors are parallel and
\(\vec{j} = \alpha\vec{E}, \qquad \alpha = \dfrac{ne^{2}\tau}{m}\)
This \(\alpha\) is the CONDUCTIVITY, and the relation is the microscopic form of Ohm's law. Notice that it contains only properties of the material, which is why Ohm's law holds independently of the conductor's shape.

rows.subtopic: Kirchhoff's Rules and Wheatstone Bridge
rows.stem: What is a Wheatstone bridge ? Obtain the necessary conditions under which the Wheatstone bridge is balanced.
rows.solution:
WHAT IT IS. A Wheatstone bridge is an arrangement of FOUR resistances \(R_{1}\), \(R_{2}\), \(R_{3}\) and \(R_{4}\) forming the four arms of a quadrilateral ABCD, with a cell connected across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other. It is used to measure an unknown resistance by comparison with known ones, without needing to measure any current or voltage accurately.
CONDITION FOR BALANCE. Let the currents be as marked, with \(I_{g}\) through the galvanometer of resistance G. Apply Kirchhoff's loop rule to the two loops:
For loop ADBA: \(-I_{1}R_{1} + I_{2}R_{2} + I_{g}G = 0 \qquad\text{...(1)}\)
For loop CBDC: \(I_{4}R_{4} - I_{3}R_{3} - I_{g}G = 0 \qquad\text{...(2)}\)
The bridge is said to be BALANCED when no current flows through the galvanometer, that is
\(I_{g} = 0\)
Two consequences follow at once. First, the junction rule at D and at B now gives
\(I_{1} = I_{3} \qquad\text{and}\qquad I_{2} = I_{4}\)
since no current is diverted along the galvanometer branch. Second, equations (1) and (2) reduce to
\(I_{1}R_{1} = I_{2}R_{2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad I_{4}R_{4} = I_{3}R_{3}\)
Dividing one by the other and using \(I_{1} = I_{3}\), \(I_{2} = I_{4}\):
\(\dfrac{R_{2}}{R_{1}} = \dfrac{R_{4}}{R_{3}}\)
This is the balance condition. Its value is that it involves only RATIOS of resistances: the emf of the cell, its internal resistance and the galvanometer's resistance all drop out, so none of them needs to be known, and the measurement is as accurate as the known resistances are.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem:
A proton with kinetic energy \(1{\cdot}3384 \times 10^{-14}\) J moving horizontally from north to south, enters a uniform magnetic field B of \(2{\cdot}0\) mT directed eastward. Calculate :
(a) the speed of the proton
(b) the magnitude of acceleration of the proton
(c) the radius of the path traced by the proton
[Take (q/m) for proton = \(1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{8}\) C/kg]
rows.solution:
The proton enters at right angles to the field, so it moves in a circle, and all three parts follow from that.
(a) SPEED. From \(K.E. = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\):
\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times K.E.}{m}}\)
The mass is not given directly but follows from the charge-to-mass ratio: \(m = \dfrac{e}{(q/m)} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{8}} = 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}\).
\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1{\cdot}3384 \times 10^{-14}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-27}}} = 4 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
(b) ACCELERATION. The magnetic force supplies the whole of it, and with \(\vec{v}\) perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\):
\(a = \dfrac{qvB}{m} = \left(\dfrac{q}{m}\right)vB = 1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{8} \times 4 \times 10^{6} \times 2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}\)
\(a = 8 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Writing it as \(\left(\dfrac{q}{m}\right)vB\) is what lets the given ratio be used directly.
(c) RADIUS.
\(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{v}{\left(\dfrac{q}{m}\right)B} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{6}}{1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{8} \times 2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}} = 20\ \mathrm{m}\)
The proton travels a circle of radius 20 m. The size is worth noticing: a field of a few millitesla barely curves a proton of this energy, which is why accelerator magnets are measured in tesla rather than millitesla.

rows.subtopic: Power in AC Circuits and the Power Factor
rows.stem: An inductor, a capacitor and a resistor are connected in series with an ac source \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\). Derive an expression for the average power dissipated in the circuit. Also obtain the expression for the resonant frequency of the circuit.
rows.solution:
AVERAGE POWER. With the applied voltage \(v = v_{m}\sin\omega t\), the current in a series LCR circuit is
\(i = i_{m}\sin(\omega t + \phi)\)
where \(\phi\) is the phase angle between them. The INSTANTANEOUS power is the product:
\(P = vi = v_{m}i_{m}\sin\omega t\,\sin(\omega t + \phi)\)
Using \(2\sin A\sin B = \cos(A - B) - \cos(A + B)\):
\(P = \dfrac{v_{m}i_{m}}{2}\left[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t + \phi)\right] \qquad\text{...(1)}\)
Now average over a full cycle. Of the two terms on the right, the first is a CONSTANT, and the second is a cosine of \(2\omega t\) whose average over a complete cycle is ZERO. Hence
\(P_{av} = \dfrac{v_{m}i_{m}}{2}\cos\phi\)
which in terms of rms values is the familiar
\(P_{av} = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi\)
The factor \(\cos\phi\) is the POWER FACTOR. A purely reactive circuit has \(\phi = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and consumes no average power at all: energy merely shuttles in and out of the inductor and capacitor. All the dissipation happens in R.
RESONANT FREQUENCY. Resonance is the condition in which the two reactances cancel:
\(X_{C} = X_{L} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \omega L \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \omega^{2} = \dfrac{1}{LC}\)
\(\omega = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \nu = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}\)
At this frequency the impedance falls to R, the current is a maximum, and \(\phi = 0\), so the power factor is 1 and the circuit draws the greatest possible power.

rows.subtopic: Electromagnetic Spectrum
rows.stem:
(a) “The wavelength of the electromagnetic wave is often correlated with the characteristic size of the system that radiates.” Give two examples to justify this statement.
(b) (i) Long distance radio broadcasts use short-wave bands. Why ?
(ii) Optical and radio telescopes are built on the ground, but X-ray astronomy is possible only from satellites orbiting the Earth. Why ?
rows.solution:
(a) The statement is justified by the fact that a radiating system emits most efficiently at a wavelength comparable to its own size. TWO EXAMPLES:
GAMMA RADIATION, of wavelength \(10^{-14}\) m to \(10^{-15}\) m, originates in the ATOMIC NUCLEUS, whose diameter is of just that order, a few femtometres.
RADIO WAVES are produced by electrons accelerating in a circuit, and a transmitting ANTENNA radiates most efficiently when its length is about the wavelength it is broadcasting, which is why broadcast towers are metres to hundreds of metres tall.
A third example, if one is wanted: X-rays, of wavelength around \(10^{-10}\) m, are emitted by heavy ATOMS, whose size is of that order.
(b) (i) WHY SHORT-WAVE BANDS FOR LONG DISTANCE RADIO. The Earth is curved, so a ground wave cannot reach far, and a straight line from transmitter to receiver soon leaves the surface. Short waves, roughly a few MHz to 30 MHz, are REFLECTED by the IONOSPHERE, the layer of charged particles in the upper atmosphere. Bouncing between the ionosphere and the ground, they can be received thousands of kilometres away. Higher frequencies pass straight through the ionosphere into space and are lost.
(ii) WHY X-RAY ASTRONOMY NEEDS SATELLITES. The atmosphere is transparent in two main windows, the visible and the radio, which is precisely why optical and radio telescopes work from the ground. X-rays, however, are strongly ABSORBED by the atmosphere, chiefly by the oxygen and nitrogen above us. Almost none reaches sea level, so an X-ray telescope must be carried above the absorbing layers, on a satellite in orbit.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: Write the drawbacks of Rutherford's atomic model. How did Bohr remove them ? Show that different orbits in Bohr's atom are not equally spaced.
rows.solution:
DRAWBACKS OF RUTHERFORD'S MODEL. Two of them, and both are fatal.
(i) INSTABILITY OF THE ATOM. The model has the electron in continuous circular motion, which is ACCELERATED motion. Classical electromagnetic theory requires an accelerating charge to radiate electromagnetic waves, so the electron would lose energy continuously, spiral inwards and fall into the nucleus in about \(10^{-8}\) s. Matter would not be stable, and plainly it is.
(ii) FAILURE TO EXPLAIN LINE SPECTRA. As the electron spiralled in, its frequency of revolution would change continuously, so the emitted radiation would form a CONTINUOUS spectrum. What atoms actually emit is a set of sharp, discrete LINES at characteristic frequencies.
HOW BOHR REMOVED THEM. Bohr kept the nuclear picture but added two quantum postulates. First, that the electron may occupy only certain STATIONARY orbits, in which, contrary to classical theory, it does NOT radiate; these are the orbits for which the angular momentum is quantised, \(mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\). This removes the first drawback by decree: there is a lowest orbit, and the electron cannot spiral below it. Second, that radiation is emitted only when the electron JUMPS between two such orbits, carrying away the energy difference as a single photon, \(h\nu = E_{f} - E_{i}\). Since the energies are discrete, so are the frequencies, and a line spectrum results.
ORBITS ARE NOT EQUALLY SPACED. Combining the force balance with the quantisation condition gives
\(r_{n} = n^{2}\left(\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\right)^{2}\dfrac{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}{me^{2}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_{n} \propto n^{2}\)
So the radii go as \(1 : 4 : 9 : 16 \ldots\), and the GAPS between successive orbits are
\(r_{2} - r_{1} = 3r_{1}, \qquad r_{3} - r_{2} = 5r_{1}, \qquad r_{4} - r_{3} = 7r_{1}\)
The spacing grows with n, in the ratio \(3 : 5 : 7 \ldots\), so the orbits are certainly not equally spaced but crowd near the nucleus and spread out rapidly beyond it.

rows.subtopic: Size of the Nucleus
rows.stem:
(a) State any two properties of a nucleus.
(b) Why is the density of a nucleus much more than that of an atom ?
(c) Show that the density of the nuclear matter is the same for all nuclei.
rows.solution:
(a) TWO PROPERTIES OF A NUCLEUS:
Its RADIUS follows \(R = R_{0}A^{1/3}\), with \(R_{0} = 1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-15}\) m, so nuclear volume is proportional to the mass number.
Its DENSITY is enormous, of the order of \(10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), and is the same for every nucleus, as part (c) shows.
(A third, if wanted: the nucleus carries the whole positive charge of the atom, \(+Ze\), and nearly all its mass, while occupying about \(10^{-15}\) of its volume.)
(b) WHY THE NUCLEUS IS SO MUCH DENSER THAN THE ATOM. Practically the entire mass of the atom, that of its protons and neutrons, is concentrated in the nucleus, since the electrons contribute less than a two-thousandth of it. But the nucleus occupies a radius of a few femtometres against the atom's \(10^{-10}\) m, a factor of about \(10^{5}\) in radius and therefore about \(10^{15}\) in VOLUME. Nearly all the mass packed into \(10^{-15}\) of the volume makes the nuclear density larger by roughly that same factor: the atom is overwhelmingly empty space.
(c) NUCLEAR DENSITY IS THE SAME FOR ALL NUCLEI. Let m be the average mass of a nucleon, so a nucleus of mass number A has mass \(mA\), and let its radius be \(R = R_{0}A^{1/3}\). Then
\(\rho = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} = \dfrac{mA}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}} = \dfrac{mA}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_{0}^{3}A}\)
The mass number CANCELS, leaving
\(\rho = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_{0}^{3}}\)
which contains only constants. The density is therefore independent of A, the same for hydrogen as for uranium. The physical reason is that the nuclear force is SHORT-RANGED and saturates: each nucleon interacts only with its immediate neighbours, so adding nucleons enlarges the nucleus rather than compressing it.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A double-convex lens, with each face having same radius of curvature R, is made of glass of refractive index n. Its power is :
rows.context: A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, with one or both surfaces being spherical. The focal length of a lens is determined by the radii of curvature of its two surfaces and the refractive index of its medium with respect to that of the surrounding medium. The power of a lens is reciprocal of its focal length. If a number of lenses are kept in contact, the power of the combination is the algebraic sum of the powers of the individual lenses.
rows.solution:
Power is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres, so start from the lens maker's formula:
\(\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left[\dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}}\right]\)
For a DOUBLE-CONVEX lens whose two faces have the same radius of curvature, the sign convention gives \(R_{1} = R\) and \(R_{2} = -R\), because the second surface curves the opposite way:
\(\dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{R} + \dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{2}{R}\)
Hence
\(P = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{2(n - 1)}{R}\)
The power of the lens is \(\dfrac{2(n-1)}{R}\).
The commonest slip is to treat both radii as positive, which turns the sum into a difference and makes the power vanish; the factor of 2 exists precisely because BOTH surfaces bend the light the same way.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A double-convex lens of power P, with each face having same radius of curvature, is cut into two equal parts perpendicular to its principal axis. The power of one part of the lens will be :
rows.context: A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, with one or both surfaces being spherical. The focal length of a lens is determined by the radii of curvature of its two surfaces and the refractive index of its medium with respect to that of the surrounding medium. The power of a lens is reciprocal of its focal length. If a number of lenses are kept in contact, the power of the combination is the algebraic sum of the powers of the individual lenses.
rows.solution:
Cutting the lens PERPENDICULAR to its principal axis slices it into two plano-convex halves: each keeps one of the original curved faces, and the fresh cut leaves a FLAT face.
Apply the lens maker's formula to one such half, with one surface of radius R and one flat:
\(\dfrac{1}{f'} = (n - 1)\left[\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{\infty}\right] = \dfrac{(n - 1)}{R}\)
Comparing with the whole lens, whose power was \(P = \dfrac{2(n-1)}{R}\):
\(P' = \dfrac{(n - 1)}{R} = \dfrac{P}{2}\)
The power of one part is \(\dfrac{P}{2}\).
Each half has lost one of the two refracting surfaces, so it bends light half as strongly and its focal length doubles. This is the one way of cutting a lens that DOES change its power, which is what makes the contrast with the next parts worth drawing.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: The above two parts are kept in contact with each other as shown in the figure. The power of the combination will be :
rows.context: A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, with one or both surfaces being spherical. The focal length of a lens is determined by the radii of curvature of its two surfaces and the refractive index of its medium with respect to that of the surrounding medium. The power of a lens is reciprocal of its focal length. If a number of lenses are kept in contact, the power of the combination is the algebraic sum of the powers of the individual lenses.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says only “as shown in the figure”, so the arrangement of the two cut halves IS the question. Described: a horizontal principal axis with two curved lens elements drawn on it. Withheld: how the two halves are oriented and abutted, which is exactly what discriminates the four options. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
Each half is a plano-convex lens of power \(\dfrac{P}{2}\), from the previous part. The figure shows them brought back together on a common axis with their FLAT faces in contact, so that the two curved surfaces again face outwards.
Thin lenses in contact simply add their powers:
\(P_{comb} = \dfrac{P}{2} + \dfrac{P}{2} = P\)
The power of the combination is P.
The result should be no surprise: putting the two halves back together reconstitutes the original double-convex lens, apart from the invisible join, so it must behave exactly as the original did. What the question is really testing is whether the additive rule for powers reproduces that obvious physical fact, and it does.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A double-convex lens of power P, with each face having same radius of curvature, is cut along its principal axis. The two parts are arranged as shown in the figure. The power of the combination will be :
rows.context: A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, with one or both surfaces being spherical. The focal length of a lens is determined by the radii of curvature of its two surfaces and the refractive index of its medium with respect to that of the surrounding medium. The power of a lens is reciprocal of its focal length. If a number of lenses are kept in contact, the power of the combination is the algebraic sum of the powers of the individual lenses.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem says only “as shown in the figure”, so the arrangement of the two axially-cut halves IS the question. Described: a horizontal line with two curved elements drawn above it, side by side. Withheld: their relative orientation and whether they lie on a common axis, which is what the options discriminate. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
Cutting the lens ALONG its principal axis is quite different from cutting across it. Each half keeps BOTH of the original curved surfaces, with their full radii of curvature; all that is lost is half the aperture.
The lens maker's formula contains only the refractive index and the two radii, and nothing about the width of the lens, so each half has the SAME focal length as the original and therefore the same power P. A half-lens simply gathers less light; it does not bend it less.
The figure then places the two halves one AFTER the other along the common axis, so light travelling along the axis passes through BOTH in succession. For elements in series the powers add:
\(P_{comb} = P + P = 2P\)
The power of the combination is 2P.
The whole question turns on the arrangement drawn, which is why the figure matters: laid SIDE BY SIDE across the beam, so that any given ray passed through only one of them, the same two halves would give a combination of power P.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: Two convex lenses of focal lengths 60 cm and 20 cm are held coaxially in contact with each other. The power of the combination is :
rows.context: A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, with one or both surfaces being spherical. The focal length of a lens is determined by the radii of curvature of its two surfaces and the refractive index of its medium with respect to that of the surrounding medium. The power of a lens is reciprocal of its focal length. If a number of lenses are kept in contact, the power of the combination is the algebraic sum of the powers of the individual lenses.
rows.solution:
The power of a lens in dioptres is the reciprocal of its focal length IN METRES, so convert first:
\(f_{1} = 60\ \mathrm{cm} = 0{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{m}, \qquad f_{2} = 20\ \mathrm{cm} = 0{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{m}\)
\(P_{1} = \dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}6} = 1{\cdot}67\ \mathrm{D}, \qquad P_{2} = \dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}2} = 5\ \mathrm{D}\)
For thin lenses in CONTACT the powers add:
\(P = P_{1} + P_{2} = 1{\cdot}67 + 5 = 6{\cdot}67 \approx 6{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{D}\)
The power of the combination is about \(6{\cdot}6\) D.
Both lenses are convex, so both powers are positive and the combination is stronger than either alone. Working in centimetres and forgetting to convert would give \(\dfrac{1}{15}\), which is the focal length of the combination in metres rather than its power, and that is precisely the distractor offered.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier
rows.stem: The root mean square value of an alternating voltage applied to a full-wave rectifier is \(\dfrac{\mathrm{V}_0}{\sqrt{2}}\). Then the root mean square value of the rectified output voltage is :
rows.context:
Junction Diode as a Rectifier :
The process of conversion of an ac voltage into a dc voltage is called rectification and the device which performs this conversion is called a rectifier. The characteristics of a p-n junction diode reveal that when a p-n junction diode is forward biased, it offers a low resistance and when it is reverse biased, it offers a high resistance. Hence, a p-n junction diode conducts only when it is forward biased. This property of a p-n junction diode makes it suitable for its use as a rectifier.
Thus, when an ac voltage is applied across a p-n junction, it conducts only during those alternate half cycles for which it is forward biased. A rectifier which rectifies only half cycle of an ac voltage is called a half-wave rectifier and one that rectifies both the half cycles is known as a full-wave rectifier.
rows.solution:
A full-wave rectifier passes BOTH halves of the input cycle, inverting the negative half rather than discarding it. So the output waveform has the same magnitude at every instant as the input; only the SIGN of the negative half has been flipped.
The rms value is defined through the mean of the SQUARE of the waveform, and squaring is blind to sign:
\(V_{rms} = \sqrt{\overline{V^{2}}}\)
Since \(V^{2}\) is identical for the input and the rectified output at every instant, their rms values must be equal. Hence the rms value of the rectified output is the same as that of the input:
\(V_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}\)
This is a property of the FULL-wave rectifier specifically. A HALF-wave rectifier throws the negative half away, so half the squared waveform is replaced by zero, the mean square is halved and the rms output drops to \(\dfrac{V_{0}}{2}\).

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier
rows.stem: In a full-wave rectifier, the current in each of the diodes flows for :
rows.context:
Junction Diode as a Rectifier :
The process of conversion of an ac voltage into a dc voltage is called rectification and the device which performs this conversion is called a rectifier. The characteristics of a p-n junction diode reveal that when a p-n junction diode is forward biased, it offers a low resistance and when it is reverse biased, it offers a high resistance. Hence, a p-n junction diode conducts only when it is forward biased. This property of a p-n junction diode makes it suitable for its use as a rectifier.
Thus, when an ac voltage is applied across a p-n junction, it conducts only during those alternate half cycles for which it is forward biased. A rectifier which rectifies only half cycle of an ac voltage is called a half-wave rectifier and one that rectifies both the half cycles is known as a full-wave rectifier.

options.label: A
options.text: Complete cycle of the input signal

options.label: B
options.text: Half cycle of the input signal

options.label: C
options.text: Less than half cycle of the input signal

options.label: D
options.text: Only for the positive half cycle of the input signal

rows.solution:
A full-wave rectifier built around a centre-tap transformer uses TWO diodes, and the two halves of the secondary are always in opposite phase with respect to the centre tap.
During one half cycle the end connected to the first diode is positive with respect to the tap, so THAT diode is forward biased and conducts, while the other, being at a negative potential, is reverse biased and does not.
During the next half cycle the polarities reverse, so the roles swap: the second diode conducts and the first does not.
Each diode therefore carries current for HALF a cycle of the input signal, and they take alternate halves. Between them they deliver current to the load during the whole cycle, which is what makes the rectification full-wave even though neither diode conducts for more than half the time.
Answering "complete cycle" confuses what the CIRCUIT does with what each DIODE does; answering "only the positive half" would describe a half-wave rectifier, where the single diode is idle for the rest of the cycle.

rows.stem: In a full-wave rectifier :
rows.context:
Junction Diode as a Rectifier :
The process of conversion of an ac voltage into a dc voltage is called rectification and the device which performs this conversion is called a rectifier. The characteristics of a p-n junction diode reveal that when a p-n junction diode is forward biased, it offers a low resistance and when it is reverse biased, it offers a high resistance. Hence, a p-n junction diode conducts only when it is forward biased. This property of a p-n junction diode makes it suitable for its use as a rectifier.
Thus, when an ac voltage is applied across a p-n junction, it conducts only during those alternate half cycles for which it is forward biased. A rectifier which rectifies only half cycle of an ac voltage is called a half-wave rectifier and one that rectifies both the half cycles is known as a full-wave rectifier.

options.label: A
options.text: Both diodes are forward biased at the same time.

options.label: B
options.text: Both diodes are reverse biased at the same time.

options.label: C
options.text: One is forward biased and the other is reverse biased at the same time.

options.label: D
options.text: Both are forward biased in the first half of the cycle and reverse biased in the second half of the cycle.

rows.solution:
The two diodes are connected to opposite ends of the centre-tapped secondary, and those two ends are always in ANTIPHASE with respect to the tap. Whenever one end is positive, the other is necessarily negative.
So at any instant one diode finds its p-side at the higher potential and is FORWARD biased, while the other finds its p-side at the lower potential and is REVERSE biased. Half a cycle later the two exchange roles.
The two can never be forward biased together, nor reverse biased together, because that would require both ends of the secondary to be on the same side of the tap's potential at once, which the winding forbids. So one is forward biased and the other reverse biased at the same time.
This alternation is exactly the mechanism of full-wave rectification: the conducting diode always feeds the load from the same side, so the current through the load keeps one direction while the source reverses.

rows.stem: An alternating voltage of frequency of 50 Hz is applied to a half-wave rectifier. Then the ripple frequency of the output will be :
rows.context:
Junction Diode as a Rectifier :
The process of conversion of an ac voltage into a dc voltage is called rectification and the device which performs this conversion is called a rectifier. The characteristics of a p-n junction diode reveal that when a p-n junction diode is forward biased, it offers a low resistance and when it is reverse biased, it offers a high resistance. Hence, a p-n junction diode conducts only when it is forward biased. This property of a p-n junction diode makes it suitable for its use as a rectifier.
Thus, when an ac voltage is applied across a p-n junction, it conducts only during those alternate half cycles for which it is forward biased. A rectifier which rectifies only half cycle of an ac voltage is called a half-wave rectifier and one that rectifies both the half cycles is known as a full-wave rectifier.
rows.solution:
The RIPPLE frequency is the frequency at which the rectified output rises and falls, that is the number of output pulses per second.
A HALF-WAVE rectifier conducts during only one half of each input cycle and is idle during the other. So for every complete cycle of the input there is exactly ONE pulse of output. The output therefore repeats at the same rate as the input:
\(\nu_{ripple} = \nu_{input} = 50\ \mathrm{Hz}\)
The ripple frequency is 50 Hz.
A FULL-WAVE rectifier would give two pulses per input cycle, hence 100 Hz, and that is the distractor here. The higher ripple frequency is one of the practical advantages of full-wave rectification: faster ripple is easier to smooth, since a filter capacitor of given size has less time to discharge between pulses.

rows.stem: A signal, as shown in the figure, is applied to a p-n junction diode. Identify the output across resistance \(\mathrm{R_L}\) :
