A rectifier which rectifies only half cycle of an ac voltage is called a half-wave rectifier and one that rectifies both the half cycles is known as a full-wave rectifier.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — and doubly so: the INPUT signal and the CIRCUIT are both drawn (a square wave annotated + 5 V and − 5 V, beside a diode in series with a resistor labelled R_L across the output terminals), and all FOUR OPTIONS are themselves drawn waveforms. The option text transcribed above is the only text printed beside each option — its voltage-level annotation; the pulse shape and polarity are drawing-only. Described: that the input is a square wave swinging between the two annotated levels and that the circuit is a single diode in series with R_L. Withheld: the diode's orientation relative to the output terminals, which is what decides which option is the output. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
A junction diode conducts only when FORWARD biased, and blocks when reverse biased. So the output across the load resistance reproduces whichever part of the input signal drives the diode into conduction, and is zero for the rest.
From the figure the input signal swings between \(+5\) V and \(-10\) V. Of these, the portion that forward biases the diode is the POSITIVE part, which appears across \(R_{L}\); during the negative part the diode is reverse biased, no appreciable current flows, and the output falls to zero.
So the output across \(R_{L}\) is a series of \(+5\) V pulses.
The diode has acted as a half-wave rectifier for this waveform: it has clipped the \(-10\) V excursion away entirely and passed only the \(+5\) V one, which is why the larger of the two amplitudes is the one that does NOT appear in the output.

rows.subtopic: Potential Energy of a System of Charges
rows.stem:
(i) Derive an expression for potential energy of an electric dipole \(\vec{p}\) in an external uniform electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}}\). When is the potential energy of the dipole (1) maximum, and (2) minimum ?
(ii) An electric dipole consists of point charges \(- 1{\cdot}0\) pC and \(+ 1{\cdot}0\) pC located at (0, 0) and (3 mm, 4 mm) respectively in \(x - y\) plane. An electric field \(\vec{\mathrm{E}} = \left(\dfrac{1000\ \mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{m}}\right)\hat{i}\) is switched on in the region. Find the torque \(\vec{\tau}\) acting on the dipole.
rows.solution:
(i) POTENTIAL ENERGY OF A DIPOLE IN A UNIFORM FIELD.
A dipole \(\vec{p}\) at an angle \(\theta\) to a uniform field \(\vec{E}\) experiences a torque of magnitude \(pE\sin\theta\), which tries to align it with the field. To turn it further, an external agent must apply an equal and opposite torque and do work against the field.
The work done in rotating the dipole from \(\theta_{0}\) to \(\theta_{1}\) is therefore
\(W = \int_{\theta_{0}}^{\theta_{1}} \tau_{ext}\,d\theta = \int_{\theta_{0}}^{\theta_{1}} pE\sin\theta\,d\theta\)
\(W = pE\left[\cos\theta_{0} - \cos\theta_{1}\right]\)
This work is stored as potential energy. Choosing the zero of energy at \(\theta_{0} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), where the dipole is perpendicular to the field, and writing \(\theta_{1} = \theta\):
\(U(\theta) = pE\left[\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \cos\theta\right] = -pE\cos\theta\)
\(U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E}\)
(1) MAXIMUM potential energy occurs when \(\cos\theta = -1\), that is \(\theta = 180^{\circ}\): the dipole is ANTIPARALLEL to the field, and \(U = +pE\). This is the unstable orientation, from which the least disturbance sends it swinging round.
(2) MINIMUM potential energy occurs when \(\cos\theta = +1\), that is \(\theta = 0^{\circ}\): the dipole is ALONG the field, and \(U = -pE\). This is the stable orientation, which is why dipoles align with an applied field.
(ii) Locate the dipole first. The charges sit at \((0, 0)\) and \((3\ \mathrm{mm}, 4\ \mathrm{mm})\), so the separation is the hypotenuse of a 3-4-5 triangle:
\(2a = \sqrt{3^{2} + 4^{2}} = 5\ \mathrm{mm} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}\)
\(p = q(2a) = 1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-12} \times 5 \times 10^{-3} = 5 \times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{C\,m}\)
The dipole moment points from the negative charge to the positive one, that is along \((3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j})\), while the field is along \(\hat{i}\). The angle \(\theta\) between them therefore has
\(\sin\theta = \dfrac{4}{5}\)
Hence
\(\tau = pE\sin\theta = \left(5 \times 10^{-15}\right)\left(10^{3}\right)\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)\)
\(\tau = 4 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{N\,m}\)
DIRECTION. The torque is \(\vec{p} \times \vec{E}\), and \((3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}) \times \hat{i} = 4(\hat{j} \times \hat{i}) = -4\hat{k}\), so the torque is along the NEGATIVE z-direction, perpendicular to the plane containing the dipole and the field.

rows.subtopic: Electrostatic Potential due to Charges and Dipoles
rows.stem:
(i) An electric dipole (dipole moment \(\vec{p} = p\,\hat{i}\)), consisting of charges \(- q\) and q, separated by distance 2a, is placed along the x-axis, with its centre at the origin. Show that the potential V, due to this dipole, at a point x, (x >> a) is equal to \(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \cdot \dfrac{\vec{p} \cdot \hat{i}}{x^2}\).
(ii) Two isolated metallic spheres \(\mathrm{S_1}\) and \(\mathrm{S_2}\) of radii 1 cm and 3 cm respectively are charged such that both have the same charge density \(\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi} \times 10^{-9}\right) \mathrm{C/m^2}\). They are placed far away from each other and connected by a thin wire. Calculate the new charge on sphere \(\mathrm{S_1}\).
rows.solution:
(i) Place the dipole along the x-axis with its centre at the origin, so that \(-q\) sits at \(x = -a\) and \(+q\) at \(x = +a\). Take the point P on the axis at a distance x from the centre, beyond the positive charge.
Its distances from the two charges are \((x - a)\) and \((x + a)\). Potential is a SCALAR, so the two contributions simply add, with their signs:
\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\left[\dfrac{q}{(x - a)} - \dfrac{q}{(x + a)}\right]\)
\(V = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\left[\dfrac{(x + a) - (x - a)}{x^{2} - a^{2}}\right] = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\cdot\dfrac{2a}{x^{2} - a^{2}}\)
Since \(p = q(2a)\),
\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\cdot\dfrac{p}{x^{2} - a^{2}}\)
Now apply the condition \(x \gg a\), so that \(a^{2}\) is negligible beside \(x^{2}\):
\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\cdot\dfrac{p}{x^{2}}\)
and since \(\vec{p} = p\hat{i}\) lies along the axis, \(p = \vec{p} \cdot \hat{i}\), giving the required form
\(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\cdot\dfrac{\vec{p} \cdot \hat{i}}{x^{2}}\)
The potential falls off as \(\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\), one power faster than that of a single charge, because the two charges nearly cancel at a distance.
(ii) CHARGE ON EACH SPHERE, from \(Q = \sigma \times 4\pi r^{2}\) with \(\sigma = \dfrac{2}{\pi} \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}\):
\(Q_{1} = \dfrac{2}{\pi} \times 10^{-9} \times 4\pi\left(1 \times 10^{-2}\right)^{2} = 8 \times 10^{-13}\ \mathrm{C}\)
\(Q_{2} = \dfrac{2}{\pi} \times 10^{-9} \times 4\pi\left(3 \times 10^{-2}\right)^{2} = 72 \times 10^{-13}\ \mathrm{C}\)
CONNECTING THEM. Joined by a thin wire they form one conductor, so charge flows until both reach a COMMON POTENTIAL V, while the total charge is conserved. The capacitance of an isolated sphere is \(C = 4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r\):
\(C_{1} = \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-2}}{9 \times 10^{9}} = \dfrac{1}{9} \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F}, \qquad C_{2} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{-2}}{9 \times 10^{9}} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F}\)
\(V = \dfrac{Q_{1} + Q_{2}}{C_{1} + C_{2}} = \dfrac{80 \times 10^{-13}}{\left(\dfrac{1}{9} + \dfrac{1}{3}\right) \times 10^{-11}} = 1{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{V}\)
NEW CHARGE ON \(S_{1}\):
\(Q_{1}' = C_{1}V = \dfrac{1}{9} \times 10^{-11} \times 1{\cdot}8 = 2 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C}\)
The smaller sphere ends up with \(2 \times 10^{-12}\) C, having GAINED charge, since it started with only \(0{\cdot}8 \times 10^{-12}\) C. Charge flows from the larger sphere to the smaller one because the larger began at the higher potential, \(V = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\) being larger for it despite both sharing a surface density.

rows.subtopic: Series LCR Circuit and Resonance
rows.stem:
(i) A resistor and a capacitor are connected in series to an ac source \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\). Derive an expression for the impedance of the circuit.
(ii) When does an inductor act as a conductor in a circuit ? Give reason for it.
(iii) An electric lamp is designed to operate at 110 V dc and 11 A current. If the lamp is operated on 220 V, 50 Hz ac source with a coil in series, then find the inductance of the coil.
rows.solution:
(i) IMPEDANCE OF A SERIES RC CIRCUIT. The same current \(i = i_{m}\sin(\omega t + \phi)\) flows through both elements, so take it as the reference phasor.
The voltage across the RESISTOR is in phase with the current, of amplitude \(v_{Rm} = i_{m}R\). The voltage across the CAPACITOR lags the current by a quarter cycle, of amplitude \(v_{Cm} = i_{m}X_{C}\). The two phasors are therefore at RIGHT ANGLES, and the applied voltage is their vector sum, not their arithmetic sum:
\(v_{m}^{2} = v_{Rm}^{2} + v_{Cm}^{2}\)
\(v_{m}^{2} = (i_{m}R)^{2} + (i_{m}X_{C})^{2} = i_{m}^{2}\left[R^{2} + X_{C}^{2}\right]\)
\(i_{m} = \dfrac{v_{m}}{\sqrt{R^{2} + X_{C}^{2}}}\)
so that the impedance, the ratio of voltage amplitude to current amplitude, is
\(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + X_{C}^{2}}, \qquad X_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}\)
(ii) WHEN AN INDUCTOR ACTS AS A CONDUCTOR. For DIRECT CURRENT. The inductive reactance is
\(X_{L} = \omega L = 2\pi\nu L\)
and for dc the frequency is zero, so \(X_{L} = 0\) and the inductor offers only the small resistance of its own winding.
The reason, put physically: an inductor opposes only CHANGE. The induced emf is \(\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\), and once a direct current has become steady, \(\dfrac{dI}{dt} = 0\), so no back emf is generated and nothing obstructs the current.
(iii) The lamp's own resistance follows from its dc rating:
\(R = \dfrac{110}{11} = 10\ \Omega\)
On the ac supply the lamp must still carry 11 A to operate normally, so the whole impedance must satisfy
\(i_{rms} = \dfrac{v_{rms}}{\sqrt{R^{2} + X_{L}^{2}}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 11 = \dfrac{220}{\sqrt{100 + X_{L}^{2}}}\)
\(\sqrt{100 + X_{L}^{2}} = \dfrac{220}{11} = 20 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 100 + X_{L}^{2} = 400\)
\(X_{L}^{2} = 300 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad X_{L} = 10\sqrt{3}\ \Omega\)
Finally, from \(X_{L} = 2\pi\nu L\) with \(\nu = 50\) Hz:
\(10\sqrt{3} = 2\pi \times 50 \times L \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{10\pi}\ \mathrm{H} \approx 0{\cdot}055\ \mathrm{H}\)
A coil is used rather than a resistor because a pure inductance dissipates NO average power: it drops the excess voltage without wasting it as heat.

rows.subtopic: Transformers
rows.stem:
(i) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-up transformer and describe its working principle. Explain any three causes for energy losses in a real transformer.
(ii) A step-up transformer converts a low voltage into high voltage. Does it violate the principle of conservation of energy ? Explain.
(iii) A step-up transformer has 200 and 3000 turns in its primary and secondary coils respectively. The input voltage given to the primary coil is 90 V. Calculate :
(1) The output voltage across the secondary coil
(2) The current in the primary coil if the current in the secondary coil is \(2{\cdot}0\) A.
rows.solution:
(i) CONSTRUCTION. A step-up transformer has two coils wound on a common LAMINATED SOFT-IRON core: the PRIMARY of \(N_{P}\) turns, to which the input is applied, and the SECONDARY of \(N_{S}\) turns, from which the output is taken, with \(N_{S} > N_{P}\). The coils are insulated from each other and may be wound one over the other or on separate limbs. Label the input terminals, the two windings and the core.
WORKING PRINCIPLE: MUTUAL INDUCTION. An alternating voltage across the primary drives an alternating current, which sets up an alternating magnetic flux in the core. The core carries virtually all of that flux through the secondary, where the changing flux induces an emf. Nothing but flux passes between the coils. A transformer therefore works ONLY on ac; a steady current would give a constant flux and induce nothing.
If \(\phi\) is the flux linked with each turn,
\(V_{P} = -N_{P}\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}, \qquad V_{S} = -N_{S}\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{V_{S}}{V_{P}} = \dfrac{N_{S}}{N_{P}}\)
THREE CAUSES OF ENERGY LOSS:
FLUX LEAKAGE, since not all the flux produced by the primary reaches the secondary. Reduced by winding one coil over the other on a well-designed core.
COPPER LOSS, the \(I^{2}R\) heating in the resistance of the windings. Reduced by using thick wire of low resistance.
EDDY CURRENTS, circulating currents induced in the body of the core itself, which heat it. Reduced by LAMINATING the core so the currents are confined to thin insulated sheets.
(A fourth, HYSTERESIS: the core is carried round a magnetisation loop every cycle, and the energy lost per cycle is the loop's area. Reduced by using a soft magnetic material with a narrow loop.)
(ii) NO, IT DOES NOT VIOLATE CONSERVATION OF ENERGY. A transformer raises the voltage, but it does so at the cost of the CURRENT, which falls in the same proportion. For an ideal transformer
\(V_{P}I_{P} = V_{S}I_{S}\)
so the output POWER equals the input power and nothing has been created. A transformer is a device for redistributing voltage and current, not for generating energy; in a real transformer the output power is in fact slightly LESS than the input because of the losses listed above.
(iii) (1) OUTPUT VOLTAGE:
\(V_{S} = \dfrac{N_{S}}{N_{P}} \times V_{P} = \dfrac{3000}{200} \times 90 = 1350\ \mathrm{V}\)
(2) PRIMARY CURRENT. Since \(V_{P}I_{P} = V_{S}I_{S}\), the current ratio is the INVERSE of the turns ratio:
\(I_{P} = \dfrac{N_{S}}{N_{P}} \times I_{S} = \dfrac{3000}{200} \times 2{\cdot}0 = 30\ \mathrm{A}\)
The voltage has been stepped UP fifteen times and the current stepped DOWN fifteen times, and the power is \(90 \times 30 = 1350 \times 2 = 2700\) W on both sides, exactly as part (ii) requires.

rows.subtopic: Refraction Through a Prism
rows.stem:
(i) A ray of light passes through a triangular prism. Show graphically, how the angle of deviation varies with the angle of incidence ? Hence define the angle of minimum deviation.
(ii) A ray of light is incident normally on a refracting face of a prism of prism angle A and suffers a deviation of angle \(\delta\). Prove that the refractive index n of the material of the prism is given by \(n = \dfrac{\sin\,(\mathrm{A} + \delta)}{\sin \mathrm{A}}\).
(iii) The refractive index of the material of a prism is \(\sqrt{2}\). If the refracting angle of the prism is 60°, find the
(1) Angle of minimum deviation, and
(2) Angle of incidence.
rows.solution:
(i) GRAPH. Plot the angle of deviation \(\delta\) against the angle of incidence i. The curve falls steeply from a high value at grazing incidence, passes through a MINIMUM, and then rises again. It is not symmetric in shape but it has one lowest point, and for every deviation above that minimum there are TWO angles of incidence that produce it, i and e interchanged.
DEFINITION. The ANGLE OF MINIMUM DEVIATION \(\delta_{m}\) is the smallest angle through which a ray can be deviated by the prism. It occurs at the single angle of incidence for which the ray passes SYMMETRICALLY through the prism, so that the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence, \(i = e\), and the refracted ray inside runs parallel to the base.
(ii) PROOF FOR NORMAL INCIDENCE. Let the ray strike face XY normally. It enters undeviated and travels to the second face XZ, meeting it at N with an angle of incidence i inside the glass.
In the triangle formed by the prism's apex X and the two points where the ray meets the faces, the angles are A at the apex, \(90^{\circ}\) where the ray crossed the first face normally, and \((90^{\circ} - i)\) at N:
\(A + (90^{\circ} - i) + 90^{\circ} = 180^{\circ} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A = i \qquad\text{...(1)}\)
At the face XZ the ray emerges into air at an angle r, and from the geometry of the deviation
\(r = i + \delta \qquad\text{...(2)}\)
Snell's law at that face, going from glass into air, reads
\(n\sin i = 1 \times \sin r \qquad\text{...(3)}\)
Substituting (1) and (2) into (3):
\(n\sin A = \sin(A + \delta)\)
\(n = \dfrac{\sin(A + \delta)}{\sin A}\)
(iii) With \(n = \sqrt{2}\) and \(A = 60^{\circ}\), use the general minimum-deviation formula:
\(n = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{A + \delta_{m}}{2}\right)}{\sin\dfrac{A}{2}}\)
\(\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{\sin\left(\dfrac{60^{\circ} + \delta_{m}}{2}\right)}{\sin 30^{\circ}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sin\left(\dfrac{60^{\circ} + \delta_{m}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \sin 45^{\circ}\)
(1) ANGLE OF MINIMUM DEVIATION:
\(\dfrac{60^{\circ} + \delta_{m}}{2} = 45^{\circ} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \delta_{m} = 30^{\circ}\)
(2) ANGLE OF INCIDENCE. At minimum deviation the path is symmetric, so \(i = e\) and \(i + e = A + \delta_{m}\):
\(i = \dfrac{A + \delta_{m}}{2} = \dfrac{60^{\circ} + 30^{\circ}}{2} = 45^{\circ}\)

rows.subtopic: Huygens Principle
rows.stem:
(i) State Huygens' principle. A plane wave is incident at an angle i on a reflecting surface. Construct the corresponding reflected wavefront. Using this diagram, prove that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence.
(ii) What are the coherent sources of light ? Can two independent sodium lamps act like coherent sources ? Explain.
(iii) A beam of light consisting of a known wavelength 520 nm and an unknown wavelength \(\lambda\), used in Young's double slit experiment produces two interference patterns such that the fourth bright fringe of unknown wavelength coincides with the fifth bright fringe of known wavelength. Find the value of \(\lambda\).
rows.solution:
(i) HUYGENS' PRINCIPLE states that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets which spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave, and that the new wavefront at any later instant is the common TANGENT, or envelope, to all these secondary wavelets.
CONSTRUCTION AND PROOF. Let a plane wavefront AB travel in a medium and strike a reflecting surface at an angle i, meeting it first at A. Let the far end B take a time \(\tau\) to reach the surface at C, so that
\(BC = v\tau\)
During that same time \(\tau\), the wavelet that started at A has spread back into the SAME medium, so it travels the same distance:
\(AE = v\tau\)
Draw a sphere of radius \(v\tau\) about A and the tangent to it from C. That tangent, CE, is the reflected wavefront, and the reflected rays are perpendicular to it, making an angle r with the normal.
Now compare the two right-angled triangles ABC and AEC. They share the hypotenuse AC, and
\(BC = AE = v\tau\)
so the triangles are CONGRUENT. Hence the angles opposite these equal sides are equal:
\(\angle BAC = \angle ECA \quad\Longrightarrow\quad i = r\)
The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, which is the law of reflection.
(ii) COHERENT SOURCES are two sources emitting waves of the SAME frequency with a CONSTANT phase difference between them that does not change with time.
CAN TWO SODIUM LAMPS BE COHERENT? NO. Although two sodium lamps emit light of the same wavelength, the light comes from countless independent atoms, each radiating a wave train lasting only about \(10^{-8}\) s before it stops and another begins with an unrelated phase. The phase difference between two separate lamps therefore changes randomly millions of times a second. Any fringe pattern shifts with it far faster than the eye or a detector can follow, so what is observed is the AVERAGE, a uniform illumination. This is why Young's arrangement derives both beams from a SINGLE source: the two then share the same phase fluctuations and their difference stays constant.
(iii) The two patterns are formed with the same slit separation and the same screen distance, so in
\(x_{n} = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\)
only n and \(\lambda\) differ. The fringes coincide when they sit at the same distance from the centre:
\(4\lambda = 5 \times 520\ \mathrm{nm}\)
\(\lambda = \dfrac{5 \times 520}{4} = 650\ \mathrm{nm}\)
The unknown wavelength is 650 nm. It comes out LONGER than the known one, as it must: a smaller fringe order reaching the same point means the fringes are more widely spaced, and fringe width is proportional to wavelength.
